title: Why One Word Made Witnesses See Fake Broken Glass?
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — Elizabeth Loftus & John Palmer (1974) / Pickrell (1995): Post-Event Misinformation, 'Smashed' vs 'Hit', and Rich False Memories, grounded in Elizabeth F. Loftus, John C. Palmer (1974) (Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior). Empirical findings show that in 1974 at the University of Washington, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed 45 student witnesses short driver-safety films of two-car collisions and changed a single verb in one post-film question.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how hippocampus, prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that asked 'About how fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?', witnesses estimated a mean speed of 40.8 miles per hour.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Elizabeth F. Loftus, John C. Palmer (1974). Reconstruction of automobile destruction: An example of the interaction between language and memory. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-5371(74)80011-3
- Julia Shaw, Stephen Porter (2015). Constructing Rich False Memories of Committing Crime. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797614562862
- Elizabeth F Loftus, Jacqueline E Pickrell (1995). The Formation of False Memories. Psychiatric Annals. https://doi.org/10.3928/0048-5713-19951201-07

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.

offcenter_creator_bet: Hot take: eyewitness certainty is fragile — changing one verb planted fake broken glass inside honest memories. Have you and a sibling ever sworn opposite versions of one day?
